findings.headline: £13.592m Housing Regeneration Loan increase in January 2026 with expected project delays
findings.detail: General Fund Loan facility increased materially for housing developments. The report notes 'certain developments were expected to require cash flow before the end of March 2026; however, these have since been delayed'. The loan has funded only £9.601m so far.
findings.matters: Material new borrowing commitment for housing. The delays in drawdown raise questions about project delivery and indicate the capital investments approved are not proceeding to schedule.
findings.figures: Loan facility increase £13.592m; actual spend against General Fund Loan £9.601m of £18.786m budget
findings.quote: the £13.592m increase in the Housing Regeneration Loan Facility was approved on 20 January 2026. At the time of approval, certain developments were expected to require cash flow before the end of March 2026; however, these have since been delayed

findings.headline: Major capital project delays: Stodman Street £0.928m and Yorke Drive £0.610m slippage
findings.detail: Stodman Street delayed by 'extensive delays in the national power cable diversions and other site complexities'. Yorke Drive regeneration delayed because 'Development Agreement was expected to be finalised in December 2025, however it requires a parent company guarantee'.
findings.matters: These are strategic regeneration projects. Delays indicate implementation and delivery risk, and raise questions about project management capability and external dependencies beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Stodman Street variance £0.928m; Yorke Drive variance £0.610m; total capital slippage £15.133m re-profiled to 2026/27
findings.quote: Stodman Street – extensive delays in the national power cable diversions and other site complexities. (0.928)

findings.headline: Business Rates collection fund swung from £0.692m surplus to £0.469m deficit
findings.detail: In-year movement of £1.161m deterioration. The council's share of the deficit is £0.295m. This reduces the funding available for services in future years and adds to the Collection Fund deficit being recovered.
findings.matters: Business rates are core funding for the council. This swing indicates reduced business rate yield, either from reduced valuations or appeals, which is a permanent funding pressure.
findings.figures: In-year deficit £1.161m; year-end position swung from +£0.692m to -£0.469m; council share £0.295m
findings.quote: The in-year deficit on the Business Rates account was £1.161m, which changed the overall position from a surplus of £0.692m at 1 April 2025 to a deficit of £0.469m at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: HRA tenant arrears impairment provision increased £0.207m to £0.698m
findings.detail: Total HRA impaired debtor estimates rose from £0.491m to £0.698m. Current tenant arrears impairments specifically increased from £0.091m to £0.170m. This represents growing write-offs for non-payment of rent.
findings.matters: Growing provision for tenant arrears indicates rent collection is deteriorating. This directly threatens HRA revenue and is a leading indicator of financial stress in the housing service.
findings.figures: Total HRA impaired estimates: £0.491m → £0.698m; Current tenant arrears: £0.091m → £0.170m
findings.quote: HRA – Impaired Estimates on Debtors (0.491) 0.061 (0.268) (0.698)

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account operating deficit of £0.243m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The HRA before appropriations to reserves closed with a £0.243m deficit. While reserves cover this, it indicates the housing service is loss-making rather than self-sustaining from rental income. The variance deteriorated from the prior report.
findings.matters: Housing revenue accounts are designed to be self-financing from rental income and should break even. A deficit signals either inadequate rents or cost control issues, both of which are concerns for service sustainability.
findings.figures: £0.243m deficit; HRA expenditure £26.232m revised budget vs £25.555m outturn
findings.quote: The financial outturn position to 31 March 2026 for the HRA before appropriations to reserves is a deficit of £0.243m.

findings.paper_title: 08.07.26 Going Concern Status of the Council
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will dissolve the Council into a unitary authority on 1 April 2028
findings.detail: Newark and Sherwood District Council will cease to exist in 2028 when Nottinghamshire local government reorganises into unitary authorities. Three proposals are under consideration with a decision expected in July 2026. The paper states functions will continue under the new authority, but the specific terms of transition and treatment of existing borrowing have not yet been determined.
findings.matters: A lender with outstanding debt must understand how reorganisation will affect debt servicing obligations and which authority assumes responsibility for existing borrowing. Restructurings create transition risk until terms are finalised.
findings.figures: Restructure effective date: 1 April 2028; three proposals submitted; decision expected July 2026
findings.quote: Whilst this will see the closure of Newark and Sherwood District Council, the functions and services will continue to be provided by the newly created unitary authority, and hence this does not affect the going concern status of this authority.

findings.paper_title: 08.07.26 Going Concern Status of the Council
findings.headline: Capital programme significantly underspent with 74% of variance from lending to Arkwood subsidiary
findings.detail: The capital programme approved at £36.892m was only 66% spent (£24.439m outturn) with a £12.496m underspend attributed to project delays. Three-quarters of this underspend (~£9.2m) relates to the planned loan facility to Arkwood Developments Ltd, the Council's wholly owned subsidiary, indicating that subsidiary projects are not progressing as planned.
findings.matters: Persistent capital programme underperformance and specifically stalled lending to a council-owned subsidiary signals difficulty delivering development projects or potential issues within the subsidiary, both affecting council finances and strategic priorities.
findings.figures: £36.892m approved capital programme; £24.439m outturn; £12.496m underspend; 74% relates to Arkwood loan
findings.quote: The outturn performance was £ 24.439m which represents an under-spend, due to delays in capital projects, of £12.496m. 74% of this variance relates to the loan facility with the Council's wholly owned subsidiary Arkwood Developments Ltd.

findings.paper_title: 08.07.26 Going Concern Status of the Council
findings.headline: Medium Term Financial Plan requires reserve drawdown in final two years to achieve balance
findings.detail: The approved MTFP to 2029/30 shows a balanced budget overall but requires use of the MTFP Reserve in years 2029/30 to balance due to uncertainty over Government funding. This indicates underlying funding pressure that the council will need to manage through reserve depletion rather than ongoing income.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether a council's budget balance depends on continued reserve depletion. This signals structural funding challenges that will erode financial resilience in the outer years.
findings.figures: 4-year MTFP to 2029/30; MTFP Reserve use required in final two years
findings.quote: over the four-year period to 20 29/30 the Council has a balanced budget . However, t his is does require the use of the Council's MTFP Reserve within the final two years . This is due to uncertainty over Government funding in the final year of the MTFP

findings.headline: Major projects delivery risk newly flagged with target score still to be confirmed
findings.detail: A new strategic risk (SR605) has been created specifically for 'Failure to deliver or sufficiently advance approved capital projects within the Council's Capital Programme and Community Plan prior to mandated funding deadlines and/or the end of Newark & Sherwood District Council.' The target risk score is still 'to be confirmed at next review', indicating uncertainty about the scale of this risk.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage or project failure impacts financial forecasting, reserve management, and the council's ability to deliver planned capital investment.
findings.figures: New risk SR605 introduced; Capital programme referenced; Grant funding agreements mentioned as controls
findings.quote: Failure to deliver or sufficiently advance approved capital projects within the Council's Capital Programme and Community Plan prior to mandated funding deadlines and/or the end of Newark & Sherwood District Council.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation introduced as new strategic risk, currently above council target
findings.detail: Newark & Sherwood is undergoing reorganisation into a new unitary authority. This is now a formal strategic risk because of stated pressures on workforce capacity, operational resilience, and the ability to maintain business-as-usual during transition. The risk score is 'Not yet at SLT target score'. Key trigger events include loss of key staff, disruption to critical services, and governance uncertainties during the shadow authority phase.
findings.matters: Organisational restructuring creates material risk to financial controls, service delivery, staffing stability, and the council's ability to manage debt during a critical transition period.
findings.figures: May 2027 elections for shadow authority mentioned; Vesting day implied; Reorganisation of nine councils into one unitary
findings.quote: To ensure smooth transition maintaining effective business as usual (BAU) delivery while implementing significant change.

findings.headline: HRA financial sustainability risk not at SLT target score
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account risk score remains static but is explicitly noted as 'Not yet at SLT target score', meaning it sits above the council's own acceptable threshold. The HRA finances are a major revenue stream for the council, and this indicates the housing account is carrying more financial risk than management considers tolerable.
findings.matters: HRA financial stress directly affects the council's overall financial position and debt servicing capacity, both key lending concerns.
findings.figures: Current risk score marked above target score for SR602; Council owns and manages housing stock through HRA
findings.quote: Risk score has remained static. Not yet at SLT target score.

findings.headline: The council is maintaining an under-borrowed position, betting that long-term interest rates will fall from current elevated levels (5.38-5.40% for 10-year PWLB borrowing).
findings.detail: Rather than borrowing now to fund capital needs, the council is using reserves as 'internal borrowing'. The strategy document states this approach is 'prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels'. However, if rates do not fall as forecast, the council will borrow the required £43m at current high rates, materially increasing debt costs.
findings.matters: This is a material interest rate bet. With shrinking reserves and rising debt requirements, higher-than-forecast borrowing costs would strain affordability. A lender would be concerned if rates remain elevated when the council is forced to borrow.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB Certainty Rate 5.38% (01/04/2025), 5.53% (30/09/2025), averaging 5.40% for the period; 25-year average 6.11%
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by tighter near-term monetary policy.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing capacity has dropped 73% in one year, to only £2.3m additional capacity by 2026/27, due to Interest Cover Ratio constraints.
findings.detail: The council uses an Interest Cover Ratio of 1.50 to set HRA borrowing limits. Additional capacity was £8.5m in 2025/26 but falls to £2.7m in 2026/27 and £2.3m in 2028/29. With the HRA CFR growing from £109m to £143m, this tight constraint leaves little room for error if rental income disappoints or operating costs rise.
findings.matters: The HRA is a major part of the council's balance sheet (40% of total CFR). Constrained HRA borrowing severely limits the council's overall flexibility and means minimal buffer if housing operations underperform.
findings.quote: the maximum additional debt capacity set is £2.308m in order to maintain affordability in each financial year

findings.headline: The council's capital financing requirement is growing 48% to £198.9m, requiring minimum additional borrowing of £43m over the forecast period.
findings.detail: The CFR (underlying borrowing need) is rising from £146.7m to £217.0m due to the capital programme, while external borrowing actually falls from £108.9m to £85.7m. The council explicitly acknowledges it 'will be required to borrow up to a minimum of an additional £43m over the forecast period'. This new borrowing will occur at current elevated rates (10-year PWLB at 5.38-5.40%).
findings.matters: Material increase in borrowing requirements on top of existing debt raises leverage and debt-servicing costs. A lender would be concerned whether the council can afford higher interest costs as rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: CFR £146.7m (2024/25) → £198.9m (2026/27) → £217.0m (2028/29); external borrowing £108.9m → £100.8m → £85.7m; minimum additional borrowing £43m
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the proposed capital programme and diminishing investments and will therefore be required to borrow up to a minimum of an additional £43m over the forecast period.

findings.headline: Usable reserves will fall by 51% over four years while capital investment grows, from £68.5m to £33.2m.
findings.detail: The council is using reserves to fund capital spending, with Major Repairs Reserve alone drawn down by £20.2m in 2026/27. By 2028/29, usable reserves will be less than half their current level. This erodes the financial cushion available to absorb unexpected costs or service disruptions.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility and resilience. A lender would be concerned that the council is simultaneously expanding its capital programme and eroding its financial buffer.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £68.5m (2024/25) declining to £33.2m (2028/29); Major Repairs Reserve drawdown £20.2m (2026/27), £6.1m (2027/28), £1.7m (2028/29)

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs at 30.69% of net revenue stream in 2026/27; General Fund at negative 10.56% but tracking worse
findings.detail: HRA financing costs (interest, depreciation, debt repayment net of income) are projected at £9.894m against net revenue of £32.224m — a ratio of 30.69%. This burden is high and makes the HRA vulnerable to any revenue pressure. The General Fund has negative financing costs (-10.56% in 2026/27, meaning investment income exceeds borrowing costs), but this position deteriorates to -13.62% in 2027/28 and -18.34% in 2028/29, driven by falling investment income as reserves deplete.
findings.matters: HRA at 30.69% is a stress indicator if rent collection or occupancy declines, or if maintenance costs rise. The GF's apparent 'negative cost' is an accounting artefact of holding investments; as reserves fall, this advantage evaporates, and the GF will face actual interest costs in the forward years.
findings.figures: HRA 2026/27: interest £4.281m, depreciation £6.364m, MRR contributions -£700k, investment income -£51k. Total £9.894m. Net revenue stream £32.224m (implied). GF financing costs 2026/27: -1.458m on revenue stream of 13.810m (net revenue).
findings.quote: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream ... Housing Revenue Account Interest Payable 4,281 ... Proportion of net revenue stream 30.69%

findings.headline: Investment holdings declining sharply: treasury investments falling from £54.975m to £38.979m over one year
findings.detail: Short-term treasury investments are forecast to drop from £43.980m (2025/26) to £27.285m (2026/27). This 38% fall in liquid cash reserves is expected to continue, with holdings projected at £37.089m by 2027/28 and £33.716m by 2028/29. This mirrors the capital spend spike: reserves are being deployed for capex funding.
findings.matters: Declining investment income will hit the General Fund revenue budget if interest rates normalize downward. The council is currently receiving £2.598m investment income on GF, which offsets its borrowing costs; as reserves fall, this buffer shrinks. A lender needs visibility on cash and liquidity runway.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement projected to rise £24.8m in 2026/27, reaching £198.946m by year-end
findings.detail: The CFR (cumulative amount of past capital expenditure still financed by debt) increases from £173.959m (2025/26 forecast) to £198.946m (2026/27). This is driven by £28.839m new borrowing, offset only by £3.044m HRA debt repayment and £807k General Fund MRP. The CFR continues rising to £213.221m in 2027/28 and £217.034m in 2028/29, suggesting the council is in a multi-year cycle of increasing leverage.
findings.matters: CFR growth signals the council is accumulating debt faster than it is repaying it. While the council has headroom (£98.135m under-borrowing against the CFR), the upward trajectory is important for long-term debt sustainability and future borrowing capacity.
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £24.8m during 2026/27. Based on the above figures for expenditure and financing, the Council's estimated CFR is as follows

findings.headline: Capital expenditure jumps to £69.989m in 2026/27, then falls sharply to £40.297m and £19.306m
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme almost triples from £19.826m (2025/26) to £40.047m (2026/27), before dropping back to £15.623m (2027/28). The total capital programme for 2026/27 is £69.989m. The strategy does not explain the causes or drivers of this peak or whether projects are committed or at risk of slippage.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what drives a £30m swing in annual capital expenditure and whether the 2026/27 peak is locked in or depends on uncertain conditions (grant funding, partner contributions, project readiness). Slippage would require reforecasting.
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the Council is planning capital expenditure of £69.989m as summarised below

findings.headline: Arkwood Developments Ltd, a wholly owned council company, is forecasting a pre-tax loss of £77k.
findings.detail: The council exercises shareholder oversight of Arkwood through the Executive Shareholder Committee. The company 'progressed housing delivery with 89 homes completed and 149 plots commenced, but reported a forecast pre-tax loss of £77k, reflecting the need for continued focus on cost control and sales performance.' While modest, this loss demonstrates operational strain in a subsidiary dependent on market conditions.
findings.matters: Wholly owned subsidiaries are contingent liabilities. Arkwood's losses drain council resources and may require future capital injections or loan guarantees. Combined with outer-year funding gaps of £4.3-4.6m, this adds financial pressure to the council.
findings.figures: £77k forecast pre-tax loss, 89 homes completed, 149 plots commenced
findings.quote: Arkwood progressed housing delivery with 89 homes completed and 149 plots commenced, but reported a forecast pre-tax loss of £77k, reflecting the need for continued focus on cost control and sales performance.

findings.headline: Internal Audit identified Limited Assurance on Business Continuity, signalling weaknesses in resilience planning.
findings.detail: Of 13 internal audit reviews conducted in 2024/25, two received Limited Assurance ratings: Business Continuity and Equality, Diversity and Inclusion. The auditor notes this highlights 'weaknesses in resilience planning'. This suggests the council lacks adequate contingency arrangements to maintain service delivery and financial operations during a crisis.
findings.matters: A lender depends on the council's operational resilience. Weak business continuity planning means the council could be unable to collect revenues or meet payment obligations during a cyber attack, facility failure, or staffing emergency.
findings.figures: Of 13 reviews: 4 Substantial Assurance, 4 Reasonable, 2 Limited Assurance, 3 advisory
findings.quote: two areas—Business Continuity and Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) —were rated Limited Assurance, highlighting weaknesses in resilience planning and inclusivity governance.

findings.headline: The council underspent its capital programme by £8.78m (27% of HRA capital spend) in 2024/25 due to timing and slippage.
findings.detail: On the capital side, spending was £32.936m 'with an £8.780 million underspend attributed to timing and slippage.' This material underspend signals that the council may struggle to execute its £149m capital programme on time, potentially affecting benefit realization and revenue generation timelines.
findings.matters: Capital delivery slippage delays when the council realizes income or benefits from investments and postpones when borrowing actually crystallizes. It also indicates project execution risk.
findings.figures: £32.936m spent, £8.780m underspend (26.7% of HRA capital spend)
findings.quote: On the capital side, £32.936 million was spent, with an £8.780 million underspend attributed to timing and slippage.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased 8.4% in 2024/25, showing growing reliance on borrowing for capital investment.
findings.detail: The council's CFR increased 8.4% in 2024/25, indicating 'a greater reliance on borrowing to fund capital investment'. The capital programme includes £81.8m in planned borrowing across General Fund and HRA over 2024/25-2027/28. The auditor specifically notes risks including 'dependency on borrowing (particularly within the HRA), reliance on external grants, and limited unallocated capital receipts'.
findings.matters: Increasing borrowing dependency while facing outer-year funding pressures limits financial flexibility. The specific flagging of HRA borrowing risk is concerning, as housing authorities have limited capacity to cut HRA services without legal consequences.
findings.figures: £23.457m capital expenditure 2024/25, 8.4% CFR increase, £81.8m planned borrowing, £149m total capital programme 2024/25-2027/28
findings.quote: The increase in the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) by 8.4% in 2024/25 indicates a greater reliance on borrowing to fund capital investment.

findings.headline: The council faces structural funding gaps of £4.3m and £4.6m in 2026/27 and 2027/28, dependent on delivering £8.843m in savings.
findings.detail: The council moved from a previously forecast shortfall of £1.627m to a 'fully funded position through to 2028/29', but only by identifying and committing to £8.843m in savings and mitigations. The MTFP still projects 'funding gaps of £4.3 million in 2026/27 and £4.6 million in 2027/28' which the auditor emphasizes 'underline the importance of delivering these measures and continuing to identify further efficiencies and income opportunities to maintain long-term sustainability.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can meet its obligations. Structural gaps three years out mean the council must execute significant savings or secure additional income/borrowing. If these fail to materialize, the council's financial position deteriorates rapidly.
findings.figures: £1.627m (previous forecast shortfall), £8.843m (identified savings/mitigations), £4.3m (2026/27 gap), £4.6m (2027/28 gap)
findings.quote: projected funding gaps of £4.3 million in 2026/27 and £4.6 million in 2027/28 underline the importance of delivering these measures and continuing to identify further efficiencies and income opportunities to maintain long-term sustainability.
